newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan urged to ease taxes to help govt bond market.
newsitem.headline: Japan urged to ease taxes to help govt bond market.

text.p: Japan should waive or scrap taxes relating to Japanese government bonds in order to make the market more attractive, especially to foreign investors, bond experts say.

William Campbell, Fixed Income Strategist for J.P. Morgan in Tokyo, said more foreign investors would buy JGBs if the Ministry of Finance (MOF) gave non-resident financial institutions a special exemption from withholding taxes.

The withholding tax, levied on bond income, has forced non-resident financial institutions to bear a settlement risk which many find intolerable, Campbell said. Non-resident financial institutions are those without offices in Tokyo.
To avoid the tax, some fail to register as holders of the bonds, leading to risks of being left out of pocket.
Others in the industry are also calling for a tax on securities transactions to be scrapped altogether to boost trade in Japanese government debt.
Taxes on financial transactions are among the issues the government aims to tackle as part of its plans to deregulate the Japanese economy.
Most JGB trades in overseas markets, particularly London, are settled by exchanging cash for documents that merely prove the bonds are "good" and registered at the Bank of Japan (BOJ).

Under Japan's system, Name Registration Form (NRF) documents are supposed to be sent to the BOJ reporting a change of ownership. This means traders face a risk that the officially registered owners of the JGBs could go bankrupt and the unregistered trade would be void.
"Half the accounts we visited in Europe this summer refused to buy JGBs because of credit risks inherent in NRF settlement," J.P. Morgan's Campbell said.

An official at the Japan Bond Trading Co said the two biggest hindrances to trade are the lack of a withholding tax exemption and the securities transaction tax. Japan levies a 0.01 yen tax on every 100 yen worth of yen bond sales by brokers and 0.03 yen on sales by non-brokers.
"By abolishing these forms of taxation we can prevent the escape of trade to overseas markets," the official said.

In a bid to reverse that process, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto unveiled a five-year financial reform plan this week. Meanwhile, the vice finance minister said taxes related to the financial system would be reviewed as part of a tax overhaul.

J.P. Morgan's Campbell also said waiving the withholding tax for non-residents is important if MOF is serious about switching to a T+3 settlement system. Under a T+3 system, settlement would take place three days after the trade date, rather than seven days under the current T+7 system.
The Japan Bond Trading official said a switch to T+3 is possible without abolishing the withholding tax if non-resident financial institutions are excluded from the system.
The authorities may decide to disregard the needs of foreign financial institutions if they feel tax revenues are too important to give up, the official said.
But J.P. Morgan's Campbell said the ministry cannot afford to be indifferent to the interests of foreign investors.

"They know that they have to sell a lot more bonds. Tax revenue shortfalls, more fiscal stimulus packages, they all point to the need for greater issuance. The more buyers you can find, the better price you can sell your bonds for," he said.

However, the Finance Ministry recently said it may abolish a law which exempts non-residents from a withholding tax on income gains from Eurobond investments. The ministry said it wants to repeal the exemption to close a loophole which allows a tax break on Eurobond purchases by Japanese investors who buy the bonds through overseas subsidiaries of Japanese firms.
